card.title: The address space that ran out

panels.text: When the internet was an experiment, 32-bit addresses were chosen. That gives about 4.3 billion of them. Running out was not an early concern.
The experiment escaped. Users multiplied, and depletion had been anticipated since the late 1980s.
On 31 January 2011, the last two unreserved top-level blocks of IPv4 addresses were allocated.
The successor is IPv6, with 128-bit addresses: about 340 undecillion of them. The two protocols coexist.

probes.question: True or false: IPv4 address exhaustion was one of the reasons IPv6 was developed.

claims.claim: Panel 1: IPv4 had 32-bit addresses, about 4.3 billion of them
claims.note: 32 bits in IPv4 also stated on the IPv6 page: 'The size of an IPv6 address is 128 bits, compared to 32 bits in IPv4.'

claims.claim: Panel 1: the internet began as an experiment; running out of addresses was not an early concern (first decade of operation)
claims.quote: Address exhaustion was not initially a concern in IPv4 as this version was originally presumed to be a test of DARPA's networking concepts.
claims.note: Quote says exhaustion was not initially a concern; the exhaustion page says depletion was anticipated only since the late 1980s.

claims.claim: Depletion had been anticipated since the late 1980s as users multiplied
claims.quote: depletion had been anticipated since the late 1980s when the Internet started experiencing dramatic growth

claims.claim: On 31 January 2011 the last two unreserved top-level (/8) blocks were allocated
claims.quote: On 31 January 2011, the last two unreserved IANA /8 address blocks were allocated to APNIC
The size of an IPv6 address is 128 bits, compared to 32 bits in IPv4.
IPv4 and IPv6 coexist on the Internet.

claims.claim: IPv4 exhaustion was one of the reasons IPv6 was developed (probe 2: true)
claims.quote: This depletion was one of the reasons for the development and deployment of its successor protocol
